blocks.content: A well layered request pipeline, middleware, request context, thin controllers, a business logic layer, buys you something concrete: every piece of it can be tested on its own, without the rest of the system running.

That property has a name: testability. It does not happen automatically just because code works correctly. It is a design choice, and this topic is about what that choice actually looks like in practice.
1. The Problem: Code That Resists Testing
blocks.text: 1. The Problem: Code That Resists Testing

blocks.content: Here is a method that generates an invoice. It works fine in production. Writing a test for it is a different story.

To test this method's tax calculation, a single number, you would also need to fake the system clock, intercept a real email being sent by a freshly constructed EmailService, and stop a PDF from actually being written to disk. All three are hidden dependencies the method creates for itself, invisible from its signature.

["The wall clock is read directly inside the method, so the test's expected output depends on what day it happens to run.","new EmailService() is created inside the method, so a test cannot substitute a fake without editing the method itself.","A static FileUtils call performs a real disk write, a side effect a test has no way to intercept."]
items: The wall clock is read directly inside the method, so the test's expected output depends on what day it happens to run.
new EmailService() is created inside the method, so a test cannot substitute a fake without editing the method itself.
A static FileUtils call performs a real disk write, a side effect a test has no way to intercept.

blocks.content: 2. What Makes Code Hard to Test
blocks.text: 2. What Makes Code Hard to Test

blocks.content: Every problem in the example above is one instance of a general pattern.

["Hidden dependencies: objects created with new inside a method, or reached through a static singleton, cannot be substituted from outside.","Static and global mutable state: shared state that tests cannot isolate from each other, one test's changes can leak into the next.","Side effects buried inside logic: a method that looks like a calculation but also sends an email or writes a file, forcing every test of the calculation to also handle the side effect.","Doing too much in one function: more responsibilities means more setup required just to reach the one behavior a test actually cares about.","Tight coupling to frameworks or infrastructure: code that only runs inside a live servlet container or against a real database connection cannot run in a fast, isolated test."]
items: Hidden dependencies: objects created with new inside a method, or reached through a static singleton, cannot be substituted from outside.
Static and global mutable state: shared state that tests cannot isolate from each other, one test's changes can leak into the next.
Side effects buried inside logic: a method that looks like a calculation but also sends an email or writes a file, forcing every test of the calculation to also handle the side effect.
Doing too much in one function: more responsibilities means more setup required just to reach the one behavior a test actually cares about.
Tight coupling to frameworks or infrastructure: code that only runs inside a live servlet container or against a real database connection cannot run in a fast, isolated test.

blocks.content: DiscountConfig.getInstance() is invisible to anyone reading the method's signature, and invisible to a test trying to control it.
3. What Makes Code Easy to Test
blocks.text: 3. What Makes Code Easy to Test

blocks.content: The fixes mirror the problems directly, and they are not new ideas introduced just for testing. They are the same layering principles this series has been building toward all along.
Dependency Injection

Dependencies arrive as constructor or method parameters instead of being created internally. A test passes in a fake. Production code passes in the real thing. Neither the class nor its logic has to change.
Pure Functions Where Possible
A function with no side effects and no hidden inputs is the easiest thing in the codebase to test, call it, check the return value, nothing else to set up.
Small, Single-Responsibility Units

A method that does one thing has exactly one thing a test needs to verify. This is the same payoff the Controllers, Handlers and Services topic described: business logic separated from HTTP concerns means testing business logic never requires a running web server.
Seams for Substituting Fakes
An interface at an integration point, a repository, an email sender, a payment gateway, gives tests a place to plug in a fake without touching the class under test at all.
A seam: production and test can each plug in their own implementation

blocks.content: 4. Unit Tests vs Other Kinds of Tests
blocks.text: 4. Unit Tests vs Other Kinds of Tests

blocks.content: A unit test verifies one small piece of behavior, usually a single method or class, in isolation, with its dependencies faked. It runs in milliseconds and touches no network, database, or filesystem. Just enough context to place it among its neighbors:

{"headers":["Test Type","Scope","Typical Speed"],"rows":[["Unit","One class or method, dependencies faked","Milliseconds"],["Integration","A class plus a real collaborator, like an actual database","Seconds"],["End to end","The whole system, through its real entry point","Seconds to minutes"]]}
Scope grows, speed drops

blocks.alt: Unit tests cover one class, integration tests add real infrastructure, end to end tests cover everything

blocks.content: This topic is about the first one specifically, and about the design choices that make the first one possible at all.
5. Mocking, Stubbing, and the Risk of Over-Mocking
blocks.text: 5. Mocking, Stubbing, and the Risk of Over-Mocking

blocks.content: A stub is a fake that returns canned data when asked. A mock is a fake a test later asks, did you get called correctly. Both let a test isolate the one unit it actually cares about from everything that unit depends on.

codes.python:
def test_invoice_applies_tax_correctly():
    repo = Mock(spec=OrderRepository)
    repo.find_by_id.return_value = Order("o1", 100.0)   # stub: returns canned data

    email_sender = Mock(spec=EmailSender)

    service = InvoiceService(repo, email_sender, FixedClock(datetime.utcnow()))
    service.generate_invoice("o1")

    args, _ = email_sender.send.call_args                # mock: verifies interaction
    assert args[0] == "customer@example.com"
    assert "118.0" in args[1]

blocks.content: The risk shows up when mocking goes further than the seams that actually need it. A test that mocks a plain value object, or every single collaborator down to the smallest detail, stops verifying real behavior and starts verifying that the mocks return exactly what the test configured them to return.

codes.python:
# Over-mocked: this test only checks that mocks return what was configured
def test_bad_test_proves_nothing_real():
    money = Mock(spec=Money)              # a plain value object, no reason to mock
    money.amount = 100.0
    money.currency = "USD"

    # The test now verifies the mock's own setup, not the real
    # behavior of Money, which could be replaced with a real object
    # in two lines and test something meaningful instead.
    assert money.amount == 100.0

blocks.content: A test like that can stay green through a genuine regression, and can break on a harmless refactor that changed nothing a user would notice. Mock at real integration boundaries, not at every object a method happens to touch.
6. Test-Driven Development as One Way to Force Testable Design
blocks.text: 6. Test-Driven Development as One Way to Force Testable Design

blocks.content: Test-driven development reverses the usual order: write a failing test first, write just enough code to make it pass, then refactor with the test as a safety net. The cycle is often shortened to red, green, refactor.
The TDD cycle
https://algorithmxlr8-assets-images.s3.ap-south-1.amazonaws.com/lld-images/1784621793455-778627536.png
blocks.alt: Write a failing test, make it pass, refactor, repeat

blocks.content: Writing the test first forces a decision about dependencies and seams before the implementation exists, which tends to produce injectable, decoupled code as a side effect. It is not the only route to testable design, though, disciplined refactoring toward the same principles after the fact gets you there just as well.
7. Refactor: From Hard to Test to Easily Testable
blocks.text: 7. Refactor: From Hard to Test to Easily Testable

blocks.content: Back to InvoiceService from section one. Every hidden dependency becomes an injected one, and the calculation is pulled out as its own pure method.

Nothing here is created with new inside a method, nothing reaches for a static singleton, and the tax calculation can be tested entirely on its own. The full method can now be tested too, with a fixed clock and a fake email sender standing in for their real counterparts:

codes.python:
def test_generate_invoice_sends_email_with_correct_total_and_fixed_date():
    repo = Mock(spec=OrderRepository)
    repo.find_by_id.return_value = Order("o1", 100.0, "a@b.com")

    email_sender = Mock(spec=EmailSender)
    fixed_clock = FixedClock(date(2026, 1, 1))

    service = InvoiceService(repo, email_sender, fixed_clock)
    service.generate_invoice("o1")

    args, _ = email_sender.send.call_args
    assert args[0] == "a@b.com"
    assert "2026-01-01" in args[1]

blocks.content: Same behavior as the original method, now verifiable in milliseconds, with no real clock, no real network call, and no file ever touching disk.
8. Common Questions About Testability
"Doesn't dependency injection just move the complexity into constructors?"
blocks.text: "Doesn't dependency injection just move the complexity into constructors?"

blocks.content: It moves the complexity somewhere visible and explicit, which is the point. A long constructor is easy to spot and easy to reason about. A hidden dependency buried three lines into a method body is neither.
"Is mocking every dependency of a service always the right approach?"
blocks.text: "Is mocking every dependency of a service always the right approach?"

blocks.content: No. Mock at genuine integration boundaries, a network call, a database, a third-party API. Real, cheap, side-effect-free objects like value objects or simple data classes are usually better left real in a test, not mocked.
"Do I need a DI framework like Spring to get these benefits?"
blocks.text: "Do I need a DI framework like Spring to get these benefits?"

blocks.content: No. Dependency injection is a design principle, pass dependencies in rather than create them internally, not a specific framework feature. Plain constructor parameters, wired up by hand or by a framework, both satisfy it equally.
"How do I know if I am over-mocking?"
blocks.text: "How do I know if I am over-mocking?"

blocks.content: A good signal: if a test would still pass after the real implementation was rewritten to do something completely different but behaviorally equivalent, the test was checking implementation details through its mocks, not real behavior.
